3.2.1.2-f132.text: Ad hunc usque diem apud nos neque mas marem, neque foemina foeminam amavit, qualia multa apud vos memorabiles & praeclari viri fecerunt: ut viles missos faciam, Hercules imberbem sectans socium, amicos deseruit, &c. Vestrae libidines intra suos naturae fines coerceri non possunt, quin instar fluvii exundantis atrocem foeditatem, tumultum, confusionemque naturae gignant in re Venerea: nam & capras, porcos, equos inierunt viri & foeminae, insano bestiarum amore exarserunt, unde Minotauri, Centauri, Sylvani, Sphinges, &c

translations.note: Burton puts this in the mouth of Gryllus, the man turned into a pig, speaking to Ulysses in Plutarch's dialogue usually called 'Beasts are Rational' or 'Gryllus'. The beardless companion Hercules chased is Hylas. Burton gives a free Latin paraphrase, not an exact quotation.

source.author: Plutarch
source.basis: text "quod apud Plutarchum Gryllus Ulyssi objecit"; sidenote "Tom. 2 Gryllo."

translations.text: To this very day among us neither has male loved male nor female female, such things as many memorable and illustrious men among you have done: to pass over the base sort, Hercules, chasing after a beardless companion, deserted his friends, etc. Your lusts cannot be held within their own natural bounds, but like an overflowing river they breed in venereal matters a hideous foulness, tumult and confusion of nature: for men and women alike have covered goats, swine and horses, and burned with a mad love of beasts, whence come Minotaurs, Centaurs, Sylvans, Sphinxes, etc.

translations.note: The speaker is Gryllus in Plutarch's dialogue (Burton's preceding text says 'quod apud Plutarchum Gryllus Ulyssi objecit'). 'Ut viles missos faciam' is literally 'that I may dismiss the common ones'. Both sentences end with 'etc.' as Burton truncates.

source.author: Plutarch
source.basis: sidenote "Tom. 2 Gryllo." and text "quod apud Plutarchum Gryllus Ulyssi objecit"

translations.text: To this day among us neither has a man loved a man, nor a woman a woman, as many memorable and illustrious men among you have done—to say nothing of the common sort: Hercules, pursuing a beardless companion, deserted his friends, etc. Your lusts cannot be kept within the bounds of nature, but like an overflowing river they breed dreadful foulness, tumult and confusion of nature in matters of love: for men and women have mated with goats, swine and horses, and have burned with a mad passion for beasts, whence Minotaurs, Centaurs, Sylvans, Sphinxes, etc.

3.2.1.2-f90.text: Ubi tu Gaius, ego semper Gaia

translations.note: This was the Roman bride's formula at the wedding. Plutarch (Roman Questions 30) gives it without 'semper' (always), so Burton has added that word.
